THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE 149

It never seems to us that he died, but just went on a journey on which we could not go, based on his article at hand, an extended appreciation of his character and work. It seems appropriate, therefore, to give the sketch of the following faculty members, based on sincere expressions of appreciation which came unsolicited to the writer from his former students.

Professor Gee's article referred to above continues with the faculty for a number of years in an attempt to rehabilitate the College and that, based on his possession, we had the impress of Mr. Halsell and Holland on the lives of the students coming here.

I have never known an educator who could inspire his pupils with greater enthusiasm than could Mr. Halsell and Mr. Holland were the men who really made the College famous in the estimation of the students. Some names to prominence from Savoy College were McLain, Thompson, of Texas. There were many men of character and virtue in Texas—great lawyers, physicians, teachers, and farmers—as well as great men and women in all the vocations of life. Since coming to Texas and since I have lived in Sherman, I have met many of his former students throughout every part of the State, one of them Judge L. A. Clark, who could tell you how much of Halsell's influence had been open his success in the law. Others rose to prominence in Texas in the same way. Mr. Simmons of Denison. There were many men whom I have mentioned, some from Denison. There were many men whom I have not mentioned from the faculty among them was George Honor in the State, and at least one of them is one of your facult members—the McLain boy—I know him and a thousand others.

If I had space I could name many others—the McMahon boy, the McMahon girl—I look back upon them and a thousand others.

${ }^{1}$ Personal letter from Mr. Sam McKee, now of Ralls, Texas, June 27, 1938.
